summary: Jesus tells of an enemy who sows weeds among a farmer’s wheat, and of an owner who lets both grow together until the harvest.
key_insight: The owner’s first concern is not the tares but the wheat. He stops his servants from weeding “lest while you gather up the tares you also uproot the wheat with them.” His patience protects the good crop.
story: Jesus put another parable before the crowd by the sea: “The kingdom of heaven is like a man who sowed good seed in his field.”
But while men slept, his enemy came, sowed tares among the wheat and went his way. No one noticed until the grain had sprouted and formed heads. Then the tares appeared too.
The owner’s servants came to him puzzled: “Sir, did you not sow good seed in your field? How then does it have tares?” He answered, “An enemy has done this.”
The servants asked, “Do you want us then to go and gather them up?” “No,” he said, “lest while you gather up the tares you also uproot the wheat with them.”
“Let both grow together until the harvest.” At harvest time he would tell the reapers to gather the tares first and bind them in bundles to be burned, “but gather the wheat into my barn.”
Jesus gave the crowd no explanation. Only later, in the house, would His disciples ask Him what it meant.

scene.label: Tares
scene.text: Most scholars identify the tares as darnel, a weedy grass that looks almost exactly like wheat while it grows. Only when the heads form can a farmer easily tell them apart. Its grain, often infected by a fungus, can make people sick.

scene.label: Tangled roots
scene.text: By the time darnel can be recognized, its roots are wound around the roots of the wheat. Pulling it up would tear out the good grain with it.

scene.label: An enemy’s spite
scene.text: Sowing weeds in a rival’s field was a known form of revenge. Roman legal writings even discuss a case of someone sowing darnel in another man’s crop.

scene.label: Bundles for the fire
scene.text: At harvest the weeds could be separated and dried, then burned as fuel, like the grass of the field that is “thrown into the oven” (Matthew 6:30).

witnesses.matthew: Only Matthew records this parable, and he alone records Jesus’ explanation of it a few verses later (13:36–43). It fits his steady attention to a kingdom that grows now but waits for a final judgment at “the end of the age,” a phrase only Matthew uses among the Gospels. Set right after the sower, it takes up a question the sower leaves open: if the seed is good, why is there so much evil in the field?

seeing.reveals: Jesus is the Lord of the field who knows exactly where evil came from and will not let His wheat be torn up by hasty hands. He has already fixed the day of harvest.
seeing.living: Evil in the world is real, and it has an author. Jesus does not ask His servants to root it out by force before the time; He asks them to keep growing as wheat and leave the final sorting to Him.
seeing.ponder: Where are you most impatient for God to deal with the weeds, and what would it mean to trust His timing there?

preaching.big_idea: Evil grows in God’s field for now, but the Owner protects His wheat and appoints the harvest.
preaching.watch_for: The servants’ question, “Sir, did you not sow good seed in your field?” (v. 27), is the question many believers ask about evil in the world. Let Jesus’ own explanation (vv. 36–43) supply the meaning of each figure rather than inventing new ones.
